author: Grok Bot (for Mateo, pending review)
description: Learn to notice how sure you are, what would change your mind, and the common thinking traps everyone falls into — then try one small move to get unstuck. Limits: Trap names are simplified labels for learning; real thinking is messier. Never used to judge a learner. Links to Decision Theory & Rationality and Self-Evolving Mind for depth.

lessons.title: How Sure Am I?
lessons.topic: Saying how sure you are (a little, pretty, very) helps you learn faster, because you notice when you were wrong and adjust.
lessons.example: Mia, 9, guessed it would rain and said 'pretty sure.' It didn't rain, so she laughed and said next time she'd say 'a little sure.'
lessons.activity: Make 5 small guesses today (weather, a score, how long a task takes). Rate each: a little / pretty / very sure. Check later and notice the pattern.
check_questions: What does 'a little sure' mean compared with 'very sure'?
Why can being wrong while 'a little sure' still be good learning?
What is one guess you made today, and how sure were you?
lessons.steelman: When is it better to act confident even if you are not very sure?

lessons.title: What Would Change My Mind?
lessons.topic: Good thinkers can name what evidence would make them change their mind. If nothing could, it is worth asking why.
lessons.example: Sam, 11, was sure his team would win. His sister asked what would change his mind. He said 'if their best player is back' — and checked the news.
lessons.activity: Pick one belief you hold (a favorite food is healthiest, a game is best). Write one thing that would change your mind, then look for it.
check_questions: Why is it useful to know what would change your mind?
What would change your mind about one belief you hold?
What could it mean if nothing would ever change your mind?
lessons.steelman: Is it ever wise to hold a belief firmly even when others disagree?

lessons.title: Looking Only for Proof I'm Right (confirmation)
lessons.topic: Confirmation means noticing what agrees with us and skipping what does not. The counter-move: look for one fact that could prove you wrong.
lessons.example: Ava, 12, thought her new shoes made her run faster and only remembered her fast days. Timing a week of runs showed a mixed picture.
lessons.activity: Choose a belief. Write 2 reasons it might be true and 2 reasons it might be wrong. Which list was harder to write?
check_questions: What is the confirmation trap in your own words?
What is one counter-move when you notice it?
Why might the 'wrong' list feel harder to write?
lessons.steelman: When is it reasonable to look mostly for evidence that supports a plan you already chose?

lessons.title: The Last Thing I Saw (availability)
lessons.topic: We often judge how common something is by how easily an example comes to mind. Big news stories feel common even when they are rare. The counter-move: ask 'how often does this really happen?'
lessons.example: After seeing a video about a shark, Noah, 10, did not want to swim. His dad helped him look up how rare shark bites are compared with other risks.
lessons.activity: Pick one scary or exciting thing you saw recently. Guess how often it happens, then find a simple fact to compare.
check_questions: Why can a vivid story change how common something feels?
Name one thing that feels common but may be rare.
lessons.steelman: When is it smart to be extra careful about something rare?

lessons.title: Already Spent, Still Stuck? (sunk cost)
lessons.topic: Sunk cost means continuing something only because we already put time or money in. The counter-move: ask 'Would I start this today, knowing what I know now?'
lessons.example: Lena, 13, kept watching a boring movie because she had already watched an hour. She asked the question and chose to read instead.
lessons.activity: Think of something you keep doing mostly because you already started. Ask the 'start today?' question and write your honest answer.
check_questions: What is sunk cost in your own words?
When is finishing something still the right choice?
lessons.steelman: Is finishing what you start an important habit, even when you are not enjoying it?

lessons.title: My Tiny Decision Check
lessons.topic: A tiny decision check: What am I choosing? What matters most? What do I know and not know yet? What is the smallest step I can undo? When will I look again?
lessons.example: Jay, 12, used the check to choose between two clubs and tried one for two weeks first — a step he could undo.
lessons.activity: Use the 5 questions on a real small choice this week. Write your answers in a few words each.
check_questions: What are the 5 questions of the tiny decision check?
Why does a step you can undo help?
When will you look again at your choice?
lessons.steelman: When is it better to decide fast without a checklist?

rationale: Everyday entry point for metacognition; matches the live Aubie Tutor thinking tools.
